title: Question 1.1
statement_text: Which finite families $F$ of digraphs are $\vec{\chi}$-finite?
context_text: Digraphs are finite and simple (no digons). A digraph is $F$-free if it has no induced subdigraph isomorphic to a member of $F$. The dichromatic number $\vec{\chi}(D)$ is the minimum number of colours in a colouring of $V(D)$ in which every colour class induces an acyclic digraph. A family $F$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite if there is a constant $c$ such that all $F$-free digraphs have dichromatic number at most $c$. This question is the digraph analogue of the study of $\chi$-bounded hereditary classes, and was first studied systematically by Aboulker, Charbit and Naserasr. They showed that every $\vec{\chi}$-finite family contains an oriented forest (a digraph whose underlying graph is a forest) and a hero in tournaments, i.e. a digraph $H$ such that $H$-free tournaments have bounded dichromatic number (heroes in tournaments were characterized by Berger et al.). They also conjectured, as a directed analogue of the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture, that $\{H,F\}$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite whenever $F$ is an oriented forest and $H$ a transitive tournament. The paper contributes results on heroes in $F$-free digraphs for oriented stars $F$, for $F=rK_1+\vec{P}_3$, and for two orientations of brooms.
notes: Stated without a parenthetical attribution in the theorem header; the surrounding prose credits Aboulker, Charbit, and Naserasr [2] with first systematically studying this question.
paper_title: On heroes in digraphs with forbidden induced forests

title: Conjecture 1.13 (Directed Gyárfás–Sumner Conjecture)
statement_text: If $F$ is a directed forest and $H$ is a transitive tournament, then $\{H, F\}$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite.
context_text: Posed by Aboulker, Charbit, and Naserasr as a directed analog of the classical Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture. The conjecture is described as wide open; even the special case where $F$ is an oriented path is unresolved. The paper investigates a weakening obtained by forbidding two specific oriented forests (brooms).
paper_contribution: Proves a weakening: if $B$ and $B'$ are valid opposing orientations of brooms $B_r$ and $B_s$ respectively, then $\{B, B', TT_t\}$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite for all positive integers $r, s, t$ (Theorem 1.16), strengthening an unpublished result of Cook and Kim.

title: Open problem: hero status of $\Delta(1,m,m')$ for degree-4 oriented stars
statement_text: Determine for which integers $m, m' \geq 1$ the set $\{\Delta(1, m, m'), F\}$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite when $F$ is an oriented star of degree $4$.
context_text: Digraphs are finite and simple: between two vertices at most one of the arcs $uv$, $vu$ is present (no digons). A digraph is $\mathcal{F}$-free if it has no induced subdigraph isomorphic to a member of $\mathcal{F}$. The dichromatic number $\vec{\chi}(D)$ is the minimum $k$ such that $V(D)$ can be coloured with $k$ colours so that every colour class induces an acyclic digraph (no monochromatic directed cycle). A family $\mathcal{F}$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite if there is a constant $c$ such that all $\mathcal{F}$-free digraphs have dichromatic number at most $c$, and $H$ is a hero in $\mathcal{F}$-free digraphs if $\{H\}\cup\mathcal{F}$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite (heroes in tournaments, i.e. in $\{2K_1\}$-free digraphs, are simply called heroes). $D_1+D_2$ is the disjoint union and $rD$ the disjoint union of $r$ copies; $TT_k$ is the transitive tournament on $k$ vertices; $D_1\Rightarrow D_2$ is obtained from $D_1+D_2$ by adding all arcs from $D_1$ to $D_2$; $\Delta(D_1,D_2,D_3)$ is obtained from $D_1+D_2+D_3$ by adding all arcs from $D_1$ to $D_2$, from $D_2$ to $D_3$ and from $D_3$ to $D_1$, and an integer $k$ in this notation stands for $TT_k$. Berger et al. characterized heroes in tournaments: $H$ is a hero iff $H=K_1$, or $H=H_1\Rightarrow H_2$ with $H_1,H_2$ heroes, or $H=\Delta(1,H_1,m)$ or $\Delta(1,m,H_1)$ with $m\ge1$ and $H_1$ a hero. An oriented star of degree $t$ is an orientation of $K_{1,t}$. Aboulker, Charbit and Naserasr showed that every $\vec{\chi}$-finite family contains an oriented forest and a hero in tournaments, and Chudnovsky, Scott and Seymour proved that $\{H,F\}$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite whenever $F$ is an oriented star and $H$ is a transitive tournament. The authors prove that if $F$ is an oriented star of degree at least 5, then transitive tournaments are the only heroes in $F$-free digraphs. They also prove that if $F$ has degree exactly 4 and $\{H,F\}$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite, then $H$ is a transitive tournament or $H=\Delta(1,m,m')$ for some $m,m'\ge1$, i.e. a vertex $v$ together with transitive tournaments $A$ on $m$ and $B$ on $m'$ vertices, with $v\to A\to B\to v$. Whether these tournaments $\Delta(1,m,m')$ are actually heroes in $F$-free digraphs is left open.
notes: Open status identified in prose immediately after Theorem 1.6; no explicit labeled environment.

title: Open problem: hero status of $\Delta(1,2,2)$
statement_text: Determine whether $\Delta(1,2,2)$ is a hero in $\{K_1 + \vec{P}_2\}$-free digraphs, i.e., whether $\{\Delta(1,2,2),\, K_1 + \vec{P}_2\}$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite.
context_text: Digraphs are finite and simple: between two vertices at most one of the arcs $uv$, $vu$ is present (no digons). A digraph is $\mathcal{F}$-free if it has no induced subdigraph isomorphic to a member of $\mathcal{F}$. The dichromatic number $\vec{\chi}(D)$ is the minimum $k$ such that $V(D)$ can be coloured with $k$ colours so that every colour class induces an acyclic digraph (no monochromatic directed cycle). A family $\mathcal{F}$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite if there is a constant $c$ such that all $\mathcal{F}$-free digraphs have dichromatic number at most $c$, and $H$ is a hero in $\mathcal{F}$-free digraphs if $\{H\}\cup\mathcal{F}$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite (heroes in tournaments, i.e. in $\{2K_1\}$-free digraphs, are simply called heroes). $D_1+D_2$ is the disjoint union and $rD$ the disjoint union of $r$ copies; $TT_k$ is the transitive tournament on $k$ vertices; $D_1\Rightarrow D_2$ is obtained from $D_1+D_2$ by adding all arcs from $D_1$ to $D_2$; $\Delta(D_1,D_2,D_3)$ is obtained from $D_1+D_2+D_3$ by adding all arcs from $D_1$ to $D_2$, from $D_2$ to $D_3$ and from $D_3$ to $D_1$, and an integer $k$ in this notation stands for $TT_k$. Berger et al. characterized heroes in tournaments: $H$ is a hero iff $H=K_1$, or $H=H_1\Rightarrow H_2$ with $H_1,H_2$ heroes, or $H=\Delta(1,H_1,m)$ or $\Delta(1,m,H_1)$ with $m\ge1$ and $H_1$ a hero. $\vec{P}_m$ is the directed path on $m$ vertices (so $K_1+\vec{P}_2$ is an arc plus an isolated vertex). Harutyunyan, Le, Newman and Thomassé showed that every hero in tournaments is a hero in $rK_1$-free digraphs. In contrast, Aboulker, Aubian and Charbit showed that if $F$ contains $K_1+\vec{P}_2$, then $\Delta(1,2,\vec{C}_3)$, $\Delta(1,\vec{C}_3,2)$, $\Delta(1,2,3)$ and $\Delta(1,3,2)$ are not heroes in $F$-free digraphs ($\vec{C}_3$ is the cyclic triangle). They also proved that $\{H,K_1+\vec{P}_2\}$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite if $H=K_1$, or $H=H_1\Rightarrow H_2$ with both $H_i$ heroes in $\{K_1+\vec{P}_2\}$-free digraphs, or $H=\Delta(1,1,H_1)$ with $H_1$ such a hero; with their negative result, this characterizes heroes in $\{K_1+\vec{P}_2\}$-free digraphs except for $H=\Delta(1,2,2)$. The present paper proves the same sufficient conditions for $\{H,rK_1+\vec{P}_3\}$ for every $r$, which again leaves only $\Delta(1,2,2)$ undecided, for both forbidden digraphs.
notes: Open status noted twice: once after Theorem 1.11 and again after Theorem 1.12.
